extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of mass/political communication, journalists and social scientists interested in agenda-setting research
extracted.subtask_description: Operational and methodological criteria used to test the agenda-setting function of mass media in a 1968 presidential campaign study, including sampling, content-analysis coding rules, measurement definitions, and analytic comparisons (agenda-setting vs selective perception).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'major' items — Television
rubrics_metrics.description: Television: Any story 45 seconds or more in length and/or one of the three lead stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to distinguish items given substantial emphasis on TV for content analysis and to compare 'major' vs 'minor' item emphasis across media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'major' items — Newspapers
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers: Any story which appeared as the lead on the front page or on any page under a three-column headline in which at least one-third of the story (a minimum of five paragraphs) was devoted to political news coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational rule to identify high-space/position newspaper items for coding; ensures consistency across print pieces when assessing media emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'major' items — News Magazines
rubrics_metrics.description: News Magazines: Any story more than one column or any item which appeared in the lead at the beginning of the news section of the magazine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies what counts as prominent coverage in weekly/newsmagazine formats for major/minor comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'major' items — Editorial Page Coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial Page Coverage of Newspapers and Magazines: Any item in the lead editorial position (the top left corner of the editorial page) plus all items in which one-third (at least five paragraphs) of an editorial or columnist comment was devoted to political campaign coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes opinion/editorial prominence as part of major-item emphasis when classifying political campaign coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'minor' items
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor items are those stories which are political in nature and included in the study but which are smaller in terms of space, time, or display than major items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the complement category to 'major' items to capture lower-emphasis political content for correlation analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding scheme — topical categories
rubrics_metrics.description: The answers of respondents regarding major problems and the news/editorial comment were coded into 15 categories representing the key issues and other kinds of campaign news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides the topical classification backbone for matching voter-stated key issues to media content; details of categories described in full report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intercoder reliability threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Intercoder reliability was above .90 for content analysis of both 'major' and 'minor' items (coder reliability exceeded .90 for salience of affect classification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliability standard reported to validate the content-analysis coding; indicates rigorous coder agreement was required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respondent selection — representativeness of precincts
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondents were selected randomly from lists of registered voters in five Chapel Hill precincts economically, socially, and racially representative of the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sampling across representative precincts was used to control for local variation and increase generalizability within the community studied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respondent screening — undecided voters
rubrics_metrics.description: A filter question was used to identify those who had not yet definitely decided how to vote—only those not yet fully committed to a particular candidate were interviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study restricted to those presumably most open or susceptible to campaign information to test media influence on perceived issue salience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching respondent issues to media actually used
rubrics_metrics.description: This study attempted to match what Chapel Hill voters said were key issues of the campaign with the actual content of the mass media used by them during the campaign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondents were asked to outline key issues regardless of candidates; media actually used by each respondent were collected and content-analyzed to ensure relevance of comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media selection based on pretest
rubrics_metrics.description: A pretest in spring 1968 found that almost all the mass media political information for the community was provided by specific sources (listed); accordingly these media were sampled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pretest determined the media universe for content collection (e.g., Durham Morning Herald, Raleigh News & Observer, New York Times, Time, Newsweek, NBC/CBS evenings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal scope of content collection and interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: The news and editorial comment appearing between September 12 and October 6 in the sampled outlets were coded; interviews were completed between September 18 and October 6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the campaign window used for both media content and respondent recall, aligning media exposure and voter judgments temporally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalization of media use (24-hour measure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of each communication medium is based on whether or not the respondent had seen or heard anything via that medium about that particular issue in the past twenty-four hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A short-term recall measure tying recent media exposure to respondent-stated most-important issue; used in analyses such as Table 6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salience of affect classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondents' answers were classified by coders as 'all affect,' 'affect dominant,' 'some affect but not dominant,' or 'no affect at all' to index the salience of affect in cognitive representation of issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affect denotes a pro/con orientation; this variable was used as a psychological locator to examine how affect relates to media use and information-seeking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of correlations to test agenda-setting vs selective perception
rubrics_metrics.description: The study computed correlations between (a) media major/minor item emphasis on issues and voters' independent judgments of important issues, and (b) between voter judgments and media items oriented to each party/candidate. Stronger correlations with all-news content supported agenda-setting; stronger correlations with own-party news would support selective perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative-correlational strategy is the primary analytic test: e.g., correlations of +.967 and +.979 reported between media emphasis and voter judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intercorrelations among media as reliability coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Correlations among different news media's coverage of major and minor items were interpreted as reliability coefficients indicating the extent of agreement among media about important political events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher correlations among like media and for major items indicate professional norms and wire-service influence; lower correlations for minor items indicate more latitude in selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control strategy — single-community focus
rubrics_metrics.description: By restricting this study to one community, numerous other sources of variation—for example, regional differences or variations in media performance—were controlled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-community design reduces confounds when matching voter judgments to local media content; authors note need for later individual-level tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of party-oriented media items
rubrics_metrics.description: Media content was analyzed both as 'all news' and as issues 'oriented to each party' — i.e., stories with a particular party or candidate as a primary referent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows comparison of whether voters match the general media composite or selectively attend to news about their preferred party/candidate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgment of media-format differences in interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The study recognizes that basic characteristics of newspapers, television, and newsmagazines differ (daily vs weekly, space vs time constraints) and that highest correlations tend to be among like media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation of agreement and disagreement among media must account for format-driven constraints (timeliness, space/time) and wire-service influence on major-story norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample size and pretest validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Between September 18 and October 6, 100 interviews were completed; a spring 1968 pretest identified the primary media sources for Chapel Hill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample size and pretest information support the study's internal validity; detailed categorization is provided in the full report available from the authors.
